name: Oxygen facial

card.summary: Pressurised-oxygen facial that infuses serums for an instant glow; no trials of the cosmetic treatment exist.
card.note: Visible effects are attributed by cited sources mainly to the serums; sourcing is thin.

quick.overview:
An oxygen facial blows purified oxygen across the skin while applying serums such as hyaluronic acid. Spas offer it for instant hydration and glow without downtime.

No clinical trials of the cosmetic treatment were found; the one encyclopedia source says evidence for the oxygen itself is limited.
quick.mechanism: A wand delivers a pressurised oxygen stream that is claimed to help serums absorb and support skin; this is not strongly supported scientifically according to the source.
quick.risks: No adverse-event data were found. It is described as non-invasive with no downtime, and is distinct from medical hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

lead: An oxygen facial is a cosmetic spa treatment in which an aesthetician passes a handheld wand over the face to blow a stream of pressurised, purified oxygen onto the skin while serums, typically containing hyaluronic acid, vitamins and antioxidants, are applied.[1][2] People book it for a brighter, more hydrated, plumper-looking complexion shortly before an event, with no downtime and the option to apply makeup afterward.[2][3]

A session usually starts with cleansing and exfoliation, then serum application and passes of the oxygen applicator, and may finish with a mask, moisturiser and sunscreen. Sessions run roughly 30 to 75 minutes and typically cost about $75 to $150, with higher figures reported in some markets.[1][2] Intraceuticals, the best-known brand, describes its applicator as creating a small hyperbaric-like effect on the skin that it says raises epidermal oxygen and helps ingredients absorb, and suggests a course of six treatments one to two weeks apart, then maintenance every four to six weeks, or a session one to three days before an occasion.[3]

Healthline reports that the idea that oxygen itself helps skin is not scientifically established and that research is mixed and largely anecdotal; some dermatologists attribute visible changes mainly to the serums, and others suggest the procedure can cause temporary redness or puffiness.[1][2] No clinical trial of cosmetic oxygen facials was located.

chain: Pressurised oxygen blown over serum-treated skin
Skin looks hydrated and slightly plumped
Brighter, smoother-looking complexion for a few days
angle.text: Clients get a same-day brighter, more hydrated look and a plumped appearance that smooths the look of fine lines, often timed before an event. Providers also claim longer-term gains in tone and collagen, which are not independently demonstrated.[2][3]

paras: Treatment typically begins with cleansing and gentle exfoliation, followed by serum application and passes of the oxygen wand, and may end with a mask, moisturiser and sunscreen.[1][2] Devices are described as delivering roughly 90 to 95 percent oxygen.[1] Intraceuticals says its facial can be combined with peels, needling or laser to support recovery.[3]

Grokipedia places the emergence of oxygen facials in the early 2000s, and credits Anthony McMahon with founding Intraceuticals in Australia in 2002, which marketed a topical hyperbaric oxygen approach. It reports popularity among Hollywood celebrities from the mid-2000s.[1]

Providers say the oxygen improves serum penetration and supports skin cells; Intraceuticals attributes ageing partly to less active fibroblasts and reduced blood flow and claims higher skin oxygen supports cell growth and collagen.[3] Its listed benefits include hydration, softer fine lines, stimulated collagen and elastin, brighter tone, less redness and fewer breakouts.[3]

Healthline reports that dermatologists are divided: some recommend oxygen facials as maintenance for younger skin, others are skeptical and believe the procedure may cause inflammation, redness or puffiness, and a professor quoted in a 2006 New York Times article was reported as calling it snake oil.[2] Grokipedia says that how far oxygen crosses the skin barrier lacks strong scientific support, and that the treatment differs from medical hyperbaric oxygen therapy, in which oxygen is breathed in a pressurised chamber.[1] Healthline adds that at-home oxygen products are unlikely to match spa results and that any benefit may come mostly from moisturizing ingredients.[2]
Healthline lists temporary redness, especially on sensitive skin, puffiness or swelling, and allergic reactions to serum ingredients.[2]
No studies found. Randomised trials of oxygen delivery in intensive care and surgery exist, but they concern breathing oxygen and are unrelated to cosmetic skin treatment.

timeline.event: Intraceuticals is founded in Australia, per Grokipedia.[1]
